column2: A striped animal with a dark bandit mask around the eyes and a fondness for rinsing things; looks as though it spends its nights as a secret inspector of dustbins.
A strong need to drink; the body's signal that it is time to find water, not another cup of coffee.
A short women's outer garment with sleeves and a fastening; the disciplined version of the cardigan, able to pull an outfit together.
The sharp piercing organ of a bee, wasp or scorpion; a small warning with distinctly palpable consequences.
A type of artistic work with characteristic features; the classification that tells one what to expect of a book or film.
Intense heat, or a high body temperature; the condition in which one wants the window open even in January.
A period of very high air temperature; weather in which the tarmac seems to recall that it was once liquid.
The gathering of ripe grain crops; the farming season when the field pays out the year's wages.
A tightly twisted band or strip; in medicine, a means of temporarily staunching heavy bleeding.
A short ornamental or official staff as a sign of authority and powers; an attribute under no obligation to be magical.
A long, narrow channel for draining water or moving loose materials; the track along which everything flows the intended way.
A man about to be married; the hero of the wedding, with several important phrases still left to memorise.
A long, thin shaft of wood or metal; a simple support, a fencing part or a gymnast's apparatus.
A large predatory freshwater fish of the carp family; it hunts small fry despite its peaceable relations.
The upper opening of a volcano, or a narrow vent; the place through which the underworld may lose its temper.
A movement of hand, head or body conveying meaning without words; the silent commentary on a conversation.
Thin sheet steel, usually coated for protection; the metal of the biscuit barrel — which, in every British household, turns out to hold sewing supplies.
A small metal or plastic counter for payment, access or tallying; a little ticket that cannot always be exchanged for money.
The form of existence of living organisms; a long story of weekdays, discoveries and unexpected turns.
A person living in a house, flat or room; the name that may one day appear on the entryphone panel.
A place intended for living in; a roof over one's head, for which one is often invited to pay at length.
A tall African animal with a long neck and a spotted coat; nature's specialist in the upper leaves.
One who cuts the grain; a worker of the harvest — and, in mythology, a grim figure with a scythe.
A professional rider in horse races; an athlete for whom lightness and a firm seat are the whole profession.
A minister of an ancient pagan cult, performing rites and offerings; the go-between for mortals and their gods.
A woman serving an ancient cult; a participant in sacred rites and a keeper of holy traditions.
An insect with hard wing cases protecting its wings; the insect world's small armoured car.
One who gathers, verifies and conveys information to an audience; the professional hunter of facts and quotations.
A running contest over a set distance; an event where the finish line matters more than the starting enthusiasm.
A large heap of fallen or heaped-up objects; also an excess of tasks beneath which the desk vanishes from view.
A precept or promise of special moral or spiritual weight; a word one is not expected to forget.
The darkening of skin under ultraviolet light; a summer souvenir that sometimes turns out to be the receipt for too much sun.
A foundation laid in advance for future work or growth; a starting capital of things already done.
Cheerful energy, keenness and excitement; the internal motor that starts a person without an ignition key.
An arrival, or a drive into a place; also one race in a competition, and the Saturday changeover at every seaside hotel.
A device for holding objects firmly; in medicine an instrument, about the house a small helper with a grip.
The disappearance of the sun below the horizon; a daily light show that charges no admission.
A binding rule established by the state; a norm whose breach may introduce one to a solicitor.
A large room for assemblies, performances or receiving guests; a chamber built with crowds in mind.
A grand formal chamber in a house or palace; a room in which even one's footsteps sound more ceremonial.
A simultaneous discharge of several guns or weapons; a loud way of announcing that proceedings have begun.
The movement of hand or implement backwards before a blow or throw; the preparation from which the decisive gesture follows.
A measurement of a parameter at a particular moment; a figure obtained from an instrument, not from the eye.
The mixing of ingredients into a uniform mass; colloquially, a tangled business with a great many participants.
A soft leather with a velvety surface; a material that looks luxurious but does not care for muddy weather.
A sideways slide of a car or other vehicle; the moment when the trajectory stops obeying the driver.
The point of the horizon where the sun sets; the direction that sits on the left of the map.
What has been set aside for the future; a stock one is especially glad of when the main supply runs out.
The opening part of a song, setting the tone of the performance; the musical start before the whole chorus joins in.
A prolonged bout of continuous drinking; a dangerous condition requiring medical help, not romanticising.
A firm promise to oneself not to do something; a private rule hard to break without a guilty conscience.
A quantity of energy, electricity or explosive; something that can power a device or set a process off.
A metal fastening bar slid across a door; a reliable barrier requiring no electronic password.
A plan or undertaking, often unusual and risky; the idea after which one's friends ask what, exactly, one has in mind.
A stretch of river sheltered from the current, usually handy for mooring boats; a watery harbour in the river's bend.
A going in, or an arrival somewhere; also one of the repeated attempts at a task.
Hair dressed or brushed in a particular direction; a hairstyle that demands discipline — and, in certain cases, a stiff breeze.
A form of knowledge assessment at a place of study; the mark that means the subject may be safely forgotten until the exam.
A swift, long-eared animal famed for leaping and seasonal changes of coat; the woodland champion of escape.
A celestial body shining with its own light; also a celebrity around whom public attention revolves.
A part of a chain, or a distinct group of people within a larger structure; the element without which the whole loses connection.
A wild mammal; figuratively, a person of unusual strength or a formidable temper.
A clear, usually high metallic or glassy tone on being struck; a sound that lingers in the air — the speciality of English church bells.
Vibrations of a medium perceived by hearing; what turns silence into music, speech or noise.
The state of physical, mental and social well-being; a capital best guarded before the doctor's appointment.
An involuntary deep breath with the mouth wide open; the body's signal that it is bored, or overdue for bed.
A prepared infusion or remedy, especially in fairy tales and old texts; a drink with a reputation for magic.
A cold dish of cooked meat pressed and set in jelly; shares its name with muscular strength, which is more than can be said for every slice.
The planet we live on, or the soil beneath our feet; a vast territory with a remarkable number of chores.
The highest point of the celestial sphere directly above the observer; the summit of position or success.
The seed of a cereal crop; the small unit of harvest from which the great loaf begins.
The coldest season of the year in temperate latitudes; the time when a scarf becomes an item of first necessity.
A plant of the grass family, to which wheat, rye and oats belong; the backbone of the bread field.
A strong feeling of ill will; the emotion that rarely solves the problem, though it reliably attends it.
A mythological or fabulous reptilian monster; sometimes many-headed, and always with a difficult temperament.
A conventional mark, symbol or indication; a small element carrying a definite meaning.
A ceremonial flag as the symbol of a regiment, organisation or idea; a cloth with history and honour attached — Britain parades its own as the Colours.
A spell of fierce, dry heat; summer weather in which shade becomes the most valuable address on the street.
A summoning sound or appeal; a signal that makes one want to answer and draw near.
The incombustible residue left after fuel or organic matter burns; what remains of a fire.
A bounded territory with particular conditions or purposes; a stretch of space with rules of its own.
A slender instrument for exploring cavities, channels or inaccessible places; a device sent to find out what nobody can see.
A folding contraption for protection against rain or sun; a portable roof with a handle — and a fixture of lost property offices everywhere.
A cutlet or roll of meat, or of potato, with a filling; a dish with a surprise tucked inside.
The ability to perceive light and see objects; the sense by which one is reading this very clue.
A hard organ in the mouth for biting and chewing; a detail especially appreciated after a visit to the dentist.
A tooth on a wheel, or a point on a notched edge such as a battlement or a crown; one element of a jagged row.
The European bison, a huge wild ox of the forests; a woodland giant rescued from extinction by patient breeding.
An unpleasant sensation provoking an urge to scratch; an irritating signal that is hard to ignore.
A member of a people living chiefly in southern Africa; a nation whose name also serves as the word for Z in the phonetic alphabet.
A wooden wind instrument with a double reed and a piercing, festive sound; the traditional voice of celebration in the East.
A light movement of the water's surface, usually without much wind; the small waves that gently rock a boat.
A field ploughed up and left over winter; the soil's way of resting before the next season's work.
A daughter's husband, or a sister's; the relative who joins the family circle by way of a wedding.
A tree or shrub with pliant branches, often growing by water; the first to unfurl its fluffy catkins in spring — and the wood of the cricket bat.
A thin, sharp metal implement for sewing or medical procedures; a small object with great piercing potential.
Harsh domination, or the subjection of one people to another; a historical word about the state of being unfree.
An activity with rules, for pleasure, training or competition; a space in which one may try on a different role.
A participant in a game or sporting contest; one who accepts the rules and aims to win.
A perfect exemplar or the highest goal of striving; a bar that reality does not always reach.
A crude word for a foolish person; historically a medical term, now obsolete in that sense and merely offensive.
An object of worship in the form of a divine image; also a person admired to excess.
The old trade of carrying people and goods by horse and cab; the taxi service of its day — the name lives on in London's licensed carriages.
A place where a straight line or surface changes direction; a turn without a corner.
A person rejected by society or a group; one for whom no place could be found among their own.
An abrupt turn in a line's direction; also the place where something snaps — the bend nobody planned.
The gradual deterioration of a part or material in service; the fee charged by long service.
A shortcoming or defect; a small imperfection capable of spoiling the whole impression.
A dried grape; the sweet morsel that enlivens porridge and baking — and hides in the bun where one hoped for chocolate.
A painted image of Christ, the Mother of God or the saints in the Christian tradition; an object of prayer and veneration.
An involuntary repeated spasm of the diaphragm with its distinctive sound; the body throwing itself a little rhythmic pause.
The picture of a person, organisation or brand in the eyes of others; a reputation one may design, but hardly control.
An adherent of India's majority religion; the word denotes religious adherence rather than nationality — a distinction worth keeping.
A large domestic bird with a bare head and a fleshy wattle; the main course of the festive table — and the anchor of every British Christmas dinner.
Crystals of ice that settle on cold surfaces; the delicate white patterning the weather draws overnight.
A sweet fruit, full of tiny seeds, that grows on a Mediterranean tree; modest in appearance, yet a whole garden within.
One who has taken religious vows in the Buddhist tradition; a man living by spiritual rule, in a cell and in prayer.
